approved_target.intended_analysis_population: All randomized participants in the comparison groups

measurement.method: Able to work, defined as having a job, being in school, or seeking work.

time_point_or_window.description: Four-month follow-up; four months after graduation for treated participants, with matched intervals for controls.

reported_result.analysis_population: 45 treated patients and 49 control patients who returned for the four-month follow-up; 94 of 106 randomized patients returned. Two treatment patients never started, seven dropped out, and only two of these nine could be contacted after four months; these patients were excluded from the analysis.

30|Because ordinary treatment is not sufficient in
31|patients with chronic low back pain, several years
32|ago a new, more active approach was tried that
33|features intensive physical training. Results showed
34|that one must exceed the pain threshold and "over-
35|come oneself' in training intensity.19"21 Not even 2
36|hours a week of intensive training for a month seem
37|adequate,19 at least not for hard-working men.22
38|However, very often, we cannot find an organic
39|explanation for disabling low back pain.23"2' Com-
40|plaints of chronic back pain often correlate poorly
41|with apparent pathology18,26 or with measured
42|physical capacities and behaviors.27"30 This obser-
43|vation suggests we ought not only to focus on the
44|physical part of the pain, but to consider the prob-
45|lem as a biopsychosocial complex, all parts of
46|which need to be addressed in treatment. In the
47|United States, Mayer et al" first proved that in-
48|tensive multidisciplinary intervention could get
49|patients back to work, a finding corroborated by
50|Hazard et al20 and-in a modified program--by
51|Sachs et al.32 However, modified programs in Nor-
52|way and Finland failed to get people back to
53|work.33,34 To our knowledge, no randomized, ob-
54|server-blinded study has ever been conducted to
55|test such an intensive multidisciplinary program
56|for this very expensive, complex problem.

112|O B J E C T I V E
113|The aim of this study was to determine whether a
114|3-week, full-time, multidisciplinary program would
115|affect the return-to-work rate, the number of days of
116|sick leave used, the number of contacts with health
117|care providers, pain and disability levels, and iso-
118|metric back-muscle endurance in patients with
119|chronic low back pain.
120|M E T H O D S
121|This parallel-group study was prospective and ob-
122|server-blinded. After an initial medical examination,
123|patients were randomly assigned to a treatment group
124|or a control group according to the minimization prin-
125|ciple'5 (a means of achieving an even distribution ac-
126|cording to sex, age, pain and function scores,36 days of
127|sick leave, and smoking status in the two groups).
128|Patients
129|The study included 106 patients referred to the
130|Copenhagen Back Center between May 1991 and
131|May 1992. Subjects had to be 18 to 59 years in age,
132|read and write Danish, have had at least 6 months
133|of disabling low back trouble, and have a threat-
134|ened job situation owing to back problems (most
135|were on sick leave or did not have a job). Most of

13|The project was blinded in that the physician
14|who saw the patients for the initial examination and
15|the 4-month follow-up did not know which group
16|each patient was in. The same physician saw all the
17|patients in both groups throughout the study. The
18|blinding was broken in about 10% of the cases,
19|equally distributed between the two groups, when
20|patients disclosed this information during the fol-
21|low-up examination.
22|Treatment
23|Our program was a modification of the functional
24|restoration programs described earlier by Mayer31 and
25|Hazard.20 The concept is described in detail else-
26|where.3' On the first day, the patients underwent
27|various tests. Physical tests included dynamic and
28|isometric endurance, lifting capacity, walking and
29|running 400 meters, and standing and sitting toler-
30|ance. The psychological tests included the Millon
31|Behavioral Health Inventory, the Million Pain Ana-
32|log Scale, the Symptom Check List 90-R, the Thera-
33|peutic Alexithymia Scale (TAS), and the Vanderbilt
34|Coping Questionnaire. A structured psychological
35|interview was also carried out the first day.
36|Each patient participated for 39 hours per week
37|for 3 successive weeks. The daily schedule is shown
38|in Table 2. The aerobics class included training in
39|cardiovascular fitness, muscular endurance, coordi-
40|nation, and stretching. This was followed by pro-
41|gressive strength and endurance training for all ma-
42|jor muscle groups, using air-moderated machines
43|and other training equipment. Occupational ther-
44|apy consisted of simulated work situations, includ-
45|ing lifting, pulling, pushing, sitting and standing
46|workplaces, garden work, and kitchen work. Bio-
47|feedback was used in some of the sitting work situ-
48|ations.
49|The psychological treatment had a behavioral
50|approach; patients were urged to take greater re-
51|sponsibility for coping with pain, set realistic per-
52|sonal goals, change the negative sensation of pain
53|into a more positive way of living, and give them-

66|Statistical methods
67|The baseline and 4-month values were compared
68|in separate analyses using Mann-Whitney tests. Be-
69|cause more patients in the treated group were able
70|to work at baseline, an additional Fisher-Irwin test
71|was done for this parameter. The level of signifi-
72|cance was defined as 5%.
73|The results are based on data collected at a fol-
74|low-up examination at 4 months (the first Monday
75|after 122 days after graduation). Each patient in the
76|control group was matched at randomization with
77|one in the treated group, so that the interval be-
78|tween the initial medical examination and the 4-
79|month examination was identical.
80|Return to work
81|One of the major goals of the project was to
82|prepare patients physically and psychologically to go
83|back to work. "Workability" was defined as having a
84|job, being in school, or seeking work.
85|At the 4-month follow-up, 29 (64%) of the 45
86|treated patients were able to work, compared with
87|12 (27%) at baseline; in the control group, 14
88|(28%) of the 49 patients were able to work at the
89|time of the 4-month follow-up, compared with 8
90|(16%) at baseline. The difference between the two
91|groups was significant (P < .001); the differences in
92|the before and after values in the two groups were
93|also significant (P < .001 by Fisher-Irwin test). Of
94|the 29 patients able to work in the treated group, 17
95|had full-time jobs, seven were unemployed but seek-
96|ing work, and five were in school. Of the patients in
97|the treated group who could not work, six were
98|receiving social pensions and the rest were still on
99|sick leave. In the control group, 10 of the 14 pa-
100|tients able to work were working full-time, three
101|were unemployed but seeking work, and one was in
102|school. Eight persons in this group were receiving
103|social pensions and the rest were on sick leave.
104|Health care, sick leave
105|The treated group contacted family doctors, spe-
106|cialists, physical therapists, chiropractors, or hospi-
107|tals significantly fewer times than the control group
108|did. They also used significantly fewer days of sick
109|leave (Table 3).
110|Pain and function
111|Patients used a scale of 0 (no pain) to 10 (worst
112|possible pain) to rate pain in the back and in the
113|legs. After 4 months, the treated group had signifi-
114|cantly less back pain than the controls, but they had
115|no difference in leg pain (Table 3).
116|We assessed function with 15 questions about
117|how much the back problem interfered with activi-
118|ties of daily living.36 The possible answers were 0
119|("no problem"), 1 ("might be a problem"), or 2 ("is
120|a problem"). Thus, the maximum total score was 30.
121|This test indicated that the treated patients were
122|doing significantly better than the control patients
123|(Table 3).

39|Previous Scandinavian studies that tested modi-

44|which is less than in our study and the US studies. In
45|addition, it consisted of passive treatment, whereas
46|our functional restoration program stressed activity.
47|Another key difference is self-responsibility: the pa-
48|tient should be responsible for his or her own situ-

current_full_D2_question_guidance.wording: Were participants aware of their assigned intervention during the trial?

official.source_locator: Full guidance p. 28, Box 6, signalling question 2.1
official.source_excerpt: If participants are aware of their assigned intervention it is more likely that health-related behaviours will differ between the intervention groups. Blinding participants, most commonly through use of a placebo or sham intervention, may prevent such differences. If participants experienced side effects or toxicities that they knew to be specific to one of the interventions, answer this question ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’.

operational.bias_construct: Whether participants were aware of their assigned intervention during the trial.
operational.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when participants knew their assignment, including when intervention-specific side effects or toxicities revealed it. Blinding participants, commonly with placebo or sham intervention, may prevent such differences.
evidence_needed: A direct report of participant blinding, open-label conduct, or participant knowledge during the trial.
operational.no_information_rule: Use no_information only after considering direct facts, indirect evidence, and trial circumstances; an absent explicit awareness statement alone is insufficient when those facts support a probable judgment.

answer_anchors.text: Participants were aware of their assigned intervention.
Participants were blinded to their assigned intervention.

considerations: Awareness is about knowledge of assignment, not whether participants completed or received treatment.

current_full_D2_question_guidance.wording: Were carers and people delivering the interventions aware of participants' assigned intervention during the trial?

official.source_locator: Full guidance p. 28, Box 6, signalling question 2.2
official.source_excerpt: If carers or people delivering the interventions are aware of the assigned intervention then its implementation, or administration of non-protocol interventions, may differ between the intervention groups. Blinding may prevent such differences. If randomized allocation was not concealed, then it is likely that carers and people delivering the interventions were aware of participants’ assigned intervention during the trial.

operational.bias_construct: Whether carers and people delivering interventions were aware of participants' assigned intervention.
operational.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when carers or intervention personnel knew assignment, including when participant side effects or toxicities revealed it. If randomized allocation was not concealed, awareness by carers and delivery personnel is likely.
evidence_needed: A direct report of blinding or awareness by carers and people delivering the intervention, plus the allocation process when it bears on their awareness.
operational.no_information_rule: Use no_information when awareness of carers or delivery personnel cannot be determined.

answer_anchors.text: Carers or intervention personnel were aware of assigned intervention.
Carers or intervention personnel were blinded to assigned intervention.

considerations: Assess the people delivering interventions, not merely outcome assessors.

current_full_D2_question_guidance.wording: If Y/PY/NI to 2.1 or 2.2: Were there deviations from the intended intervention that arose because of the trial context?

official.source_locator: Full guidance p. 28, Box 6, signalling question 2.3
official.source_excerpt: Answer ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’ only if there is evidence, or strong reason to believe, that the trial context led to failure to implement the protocol interventions or to implementation of interventions not allowed by the protocol. Answer ‘No’ or ‘Probably no’ if there were changes from assigned intervention that are inconsistent with the trial protocol, such as non-adherence to intervention, but these are consistent with what could occur outside the trial context. The answer ‘No information’ may be appropriate.

operational.bias_construct: Whether deviations inconsistent with protocol arose because of the trial context.
operational.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes only after establishing both that the change was inconsistent with the protocol and that the trial context caused it; identify both premises in the justification. Answer no or probably no when no such deviation occurred, including ordinary non-adherence outside the trial context, protocol-consistent changes, and protocol-permitted subsequent care after progression.
evidence_needed: Evidence linking the deviation to recruitment, engagement, or trial personnel and showing it was inconsistent with the protocol.
operational.no_information_rule: Use no_information when reported details are insufficient and trial circumstances do not support a reasonable probable judgment about trial-context-caused deviations.

answer_anchors.text: The trial context caused protocol-inconsistent deviations.
No protocol-inconsistent deviation arose because of the trial context.
Reported details and trial circumstances do not support a judgment about trial-context-caused deviations.

considerations: Side-effect-related compromised blinding counts only when resulting changes were protocol-inconsistent and context-caused.

Subsequent treatment, rescue treatment, or cross-over is not itself a deviation for the effect of assignment: establish both protocol inconsistency and a trial-context cause before answering affirmatively.

Neutral contrast: protocol-permitted rescue after progression is ordinary subsequent care; prohibited rescue encouraged by trial staff is a candidate trial-context deviation. Change only the protocol-consistency and cause premises before changing the reasoning.
invalid_shortcuts: unequal post-progression treatment without evidence that it was prohibited and trial-context-caused
a protocol deviation without its cause
discontinuation or crossover without protocol and cause evidence

current_full_D2_question_guidance.wording: If Y/PY to 2.3: Were these deviations likely to have affected the outcome?

official.source_locator: Full guidance p. 28, Box 6, signalling question 2.4
official.source_excerpt: Changes from assigned intervention that are inconsistent with the trial protocol and arose because of the trial context will impact on the intervention effect estimate if they affect the outcome, but not otherwise.

operational.bias_construct: Whether context-caused protocol-inconsistent deviations were likely to affect the outcome.
operational.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when the identified deviations were likely to affect the intervention effect estimate through this outcome; answer no or probably no when they were not likely to affect the outcome.
evidence_needed: A direct link between the identified context-caused deviation and this outcome or its effect estimate.
operational.no_information_rule: Use no_information when the effect of the identified deviations on the outcome cannot be determined.

answer_anchors.text: The identified deviations were likely to affect the outcome.
The identified deviations were not likely to affect the outcome.

considerations: This question concerns the deviations already identified in 2.3, not any non-adherence in isolation.

current_full_D2_question_guidance.wording: If Y/PY/NI to 2.4: Were these deviations from intended intervention balanced between groups?

official.source_locator: Full guidance p. 29, Box 6, signalling question 2.5
official.source_excerpt: Changes from assigned intervention that are inconsistent with the trial protocol and arose because of the trial context are more likely to impact on intervention effect estimate if they are not balanced between the intervention groups.

operational.bias_construct: Whether context-caused protocol-inconsistent deviations were balanced between intervention groups.
operational.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when the identified deviations were balanced between groups; answer no or probably no when they were not balanced.
evidence_needed: Group-specific counts or descriptions of the identified deviations and their comparability between intervention groups.
operational.no_information_rule: Use no_information when balance of the identified deviations cannot be determined.

answer_anchors.text: The identified deviations were balanced between intervention groups.
The identified deviations were not balanced between intervention groups.

considerations: Balance refers to the deviations identified in 2.3 and their potential effect, not to baseline group sizes.

current_full_D2_question_guidance.wording: Was an appropriate analysis used to estimate the effect of assignment to intervention?

official.source_locator: Full guidance p. 29, Box 6, signalling question 2.6
official.source_excerpt: Both intention-to-treat (ITT) analyses and modified intention-to-treat (mITT) analyses excluding participants with missing outcome data should be considered appropriate. Both naïve ‘per-protocol’ analyses and ‘as treated’ analyses should be considered inappropriate. Analyses excluding eligible trial participants post-randomization should also be considered inappropriate.

operational.bias_construct: Whether an appropriate analysis estimated the effect of assignment to intervention. Compare randomized assignment with the actual analysis population, grouping, reassignment, and exclusions, including their reasons; an ITT, modified ITT, or as-treated label alone does not establish this.
operational.decision_rule: Consider ITT and modified ITT excluding participants with missing outcome data appropriate. Consider naive per-protocol, as-treated, and post-randomization exclusion of eligible participants inappropriate; post-randomization exclusion of ineligible participants may be appropriate when eligibility could not have been influenced by assignment.
evidence_needed: The actual analysis population and grouping rule: who was assigned, who was analysed in each group, who was excluded or reassigned after randomization, and why.
operational.no_information_rule: Use no_information only after considering direct facts, indirect evidence, and trial circumstances; an incomplete analysis description alone is insufficient when those facts support a probable judgment about appropriateness.

answer_anchors.text: An ITT or appropriate modified ITT analysis estimated assignment effect.
A naive per-protocol, as-treated, or inappropriate post-randomization exclusion analysis was used.

considerations: The question is about effect of assignment, so grouping must follow randomized assignment.
Assess what the analysis actually did, not the label attached to it: ITT/mITT/as-treated terminology is a description to verify against assignment, grouping, and exclusions.

Never-treated participants are not automatically participants with no adverse event or unavailable outcome. Recover the documented eligibility, outcome availability, and exclusion reason before judging the approved assignment-effect estimand.

Excluding participants solely because their outcome data are missing can be an appropriate modified ITT analysis for D2; assess the missing outcomes in D3. An eligible participant with an observed outcome omitted from the assignment analysis, or analysed in the wrong randomized group, is a distinct D2 concern. Record whether exclusions occurred before the endpoint was measured or after an outcome value was recorded, but timing alone does not establish availability or the exclusion reason. An observed value omitted from analysis is not thereby missing outcome data. An analyzed count below the randomized count alone does not establish inappropriate analysis; if the exclusion mechanism cannot support a reasonable probable judgment, retain no_information. When 2.6 is no, probably_no, or no_information, assess 2.7 conditionally: could the wrong-group analysis or exclusions substantially affect this Result if the assignment-analysis failure occurred? Keep uncertainty about the analysis mechanism explicit. Assess potential impact using the participants affected, reasons, outcome rarity, and prognostic relevance; demonstrated actual bias or a sensitivity analysis is not required, and no precise percentage rule applies.
invalid_shortcuts: an ITT label without its population
a per-protocol label without the analysis population

current_full_D2_question_guidance.wording: If N/PN/NI to 2.6: Was there potential for a substantial impact (on the result) of the failure to analyse participants in the group to which they were randomized?

official.source_locator: Full guidance p. 29, Box 6, signalling question 2.7
official.source_excerpt: This question addresses whether the number of participants who were analysed in the wrong intervention group, or excluded from the analysis, was sufficient that there could have been a substantial impact on the result. It is not possible to specify a precise rule: there may be potential for substantial impact even if fewer than 5% of participants were analysed in the wrong group or excluded, if the outcome is rare or if exclusions are strongly related to prognostic factors.

operational.bias_construct: Whether failure to analyse participants in their randomized group could substantially affect the result.
operational.decision_rule: Assess whether the number analysed in the wrong group or excluded was sufficient for substantial impact. There is no precise percentage rule: fewer than 5% may still matter for rare outcomes or exclusions strongly related to prognostic factors.
evidence_needed: Counts and reasons for participants analysed in the wrong group or excluded, outcome rarity, and prognostic relevance of exclusions.
operational.no_information_rule: Use no_information when the potential magnitude of impact cannot be assessed.

answer_anchors.text: The wrong-group analysis or exclusions could substantially affect the result.
The wrong-group analysis or exclusions could not substantially affect the result.

considerations: This is conditional on an inappropriate or uncertain analysis in 2.6.
Assess potential impact only after deciding whether 2.6 was appropriate; a small or balanced exclusion can have low impact without making an inappropriate analysis appropriate.

Use facts about this endpoint and the excluded participants. Exclusion before outcome ascertainment may also leave outcome data missing; exclusion after ascertainment may omit observed values from the analysis. Neither timing alone settles the possible effect on the estimate.
invalid_shortcuts: a group label without exclusion counts
